title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: The mistake Alexey Alexandrovitch had made — in that, when he had been preparing to see his wife, he had overlooked the possibility that her repentance might be genuine, that he might forgive her, and that she might not die — that mistake came home to him in its full meaning two months after his return from Moscow. But the mistake hadn't arisen only from his having overlooked that possibility; it had also arisen from the fact that, until that day at his dying wife's bedside, he hadn't known his own heart. At her sickbed he had given way, for the first time in his life, to that feeling of sympathetic suffering that the suffering of others always stirred in him, and which he had until then regarded with shame as a harmful weakness. And pity for her, and remorse for having wished her dead, and above all the joy of forgiveness, made him suddenly aware not just of the easing of his own pain, but of a spiritual peace he had never known before. He suddenly felt that the very thing that had been the source of his suffering had become the source of his spiritual joy; that what had seemed insoluble when he was judging, blaming, and hating had become clear and simple once he forgave and loved.

He forgave his wife and pitied her for her suffering and her remorse. He forgave Vronsky and pitied him, especially after the reports of his desperate act reached him. He felt more for his son than before. And he blamed himself now for having taken too little interest in him. But for the little newborn baby he felt a quite particular sentiment — not just pity, but tenderness. At first, out of pure compassion, he had taken an interest in the delicate little creature, who wasn't his child and had been pushed aside during her mother's illness and would certainly have died if he hadn't bothered about her, and he didn't notice himself how attached he was becoming to her. He would go into the nursery several times a day and sit there for a long time, so that the nurses, at first wary of him, got quite used to having him there. Sometimes for half an hour at a stretch he would sit in silence, gazing at the saffron-red, downy, wrinkled face of the sleeping baby, watching the movements of her frowning brows and her fat little hands with their clenched fingers as they rubbed her eyes and nose. At moments like these especially, Alexey Alexandrovitch felt a perfect peace and inner harmony, and saw nothing extraordinary in his position, nothing that needed to change.

But as time went on, he saw more and more clearly that however natural his position now seemed to him, he wouldn't be allowed to stay in it for long. He felt that beyond the blessed spiritual force directing his soul there was another, a brutal force, just as powerful or more so, that controlled his life, and that this force would not permit him the humble peace he longed for. He felt that everyone looked at him with curious astonishment, that he wasn't understood, and that something was expected of him. Above all, he felt the instability and unnaturalness of his relations with his wife.

Once the softening effect of death's near approach had faded, Alexey Alexandrovitch began to notice that Anna was afraid of him, ill at ease in his company, and couldn't meet his eye. She seemed to want, and not dare, to tell him something; and as though sensing that things couldn't go on as they were, she seemed to be waiting for something from him.

Toward the end of February it happened that Anna's baby daughter, who had also been named Anna, fell ill. Alexey Alexandrovitch was in the nursery that morning, and after leaving orders for the doctor to be sent for, he went off to his office. When he had finished his work, he came home at four. Going into the hall, he saw a handsome groom in a braided livery and a bearskin cape, holding a white fur cloak.
"Who is here?" Alexey Alexandrovitch asked.
"Princess Elizaveta Federovna Tverskaya," the groom answered, and it seemed to Alexey Alexandrovitch that the man grinned.

All through this difficult time, Alexey Alexandrovitch had noticed that his social acquaintances, especially the women, took a particular interest in him and his wife. All of them, he observed, were poorly hiding their amusement at something — the same amusement he had glimpsed in the lawyer's eyes, and just now in this groom's. Everyone seemed somehow hugely delighted, as if they had just been to a wedding. When they met him, they would ask after his wife's health with ill-concealed enjoyment. The presence of Princess Tverskaya was unpleasant to Alexey Alexandrovitch — because of the memories he associated with her, and because he disliked her — and he went straight to the nursery. In the day nursery, Seryozha, leaning on the table with his legs up on a chair, was drawing and chattering away cheerfully. The English governess, who had taken the place of the French one during Anna's illness, was sitting near the boy, knitting a shawl. She hurriedly stood up, curtsied, and gave Seryozha a tug.
Alexey Alexandrovitch stroked his son's hair, answered the governess's questions about his wife, and asked what the doctor had said about the baby.
"The doctor said it wasn't anything serious, and he prescribed a bath, sir."
"But she's still in pain," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, listening to the baby's screams in the next room.
"I think it's the wet-nurse, sir," the Englishwoman said firmly.
"What makes you say so?" he asked, stopping short.
"It was just like this at Countess Paul's, sir. They gave the baby medicine, and it turned out the baby was simply hungry: the nurse had no milk, sir."

Alexey Alexandrovitch thought it over, and after standing still for a few seconds went in through the other door. The baby was lying with her head thrown back, stiffening herself in the nurse's arms, refusing to take the full breast offered her; and she did not stop screaming despite the double hushing of the wet-nurse and the other nurse, who was leaning over her.
"Still no better?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch.
"She's very restless," the nurse answered in a whisper.
"Miss Edwarde says the wet-nurse may have no milk," he said.
"I think so too, Alexey Alexandrovitch."
"Then why didn't you say so?"
"Who was I to say it to? Anna Arkadyevna still being ill...." said the nurse discontentedly.
The nurse was an old family servant. And in her plain words Alexey Alexandrovitch seemed to hear an allusion to his own situation.
The baby screamed louder than ever, struggling and sobbing. The nurse, with a gesture of despair, went over to her, took her from the wet-nurse's arms, and began walking up and down, rocking her.

"You must ask the doctor to examine the wet-nurse," said Alexey Alexandrovitch. The smartly dressed, healthy-looking nurse, alarmed at the thought of losing her position, muttered something to herself and, covering her bosom, smiled contemptuously at the idea that anyone could doubt the abundance of her milk. In that smile, too, Alexey Alexandrovitch saw a sneer at his situation.
"Poor little thing!" said the nurse, soothing the baby and still pacing with her.
Alexey Alexandrovitch sat down, and with a dejected, suffering face watched the nurse walking back and forth.

When the child was finally quiet and had been laid in her deep cot, and the nurse, after smoothing the little pillow, had left her, Alexey Alexandrovitch got up and, walking awkwardly on tiptoe, approached the baby. He stood still for a minute, gazing at her with the same dejected face; but all at once a smile, moving his hair and the skin of his forehead, broke out over his face, and he stepped just as softly out of the room.

In the dining room he rang the bell and told the servant who answered to send for the doctor again. He felt annoyed with his wife for not being worried about this exquisite baby, and in that annoyed mood he had no wish to go to her; he had no wish, either, to see Princess Betsy. But his wife might wonder why he didn't come in to her as usual, and so, overcoming his reluctance, he started toward the bedroom. As he walked over the soft rug toward the door, he couldn't help overhearing a conversation he didn't want to hear.
"If he hadn't been leaving, I could have understood your answer and his too. But your husband ought to be above that," Betsy was saying.
"It's not because of my husband; for myself I don't want it. Don't say that!" Anna's voice answered, agitated.
"Yes, but you must want to say good-bye to a man who has shot himself on your account...."
"That's exactly why I don't want to."

With a dismayed, guilty look, Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped and would have gone back unseen. But it occurred to him that this would be undignified, and he turned back again, and clearing his throat, walked up to the bedroom. The voices had stopped, and he went in.

Anna, in a gray dressing-gown, with a crop of short clustering black curls on her round head, was sitting on a settee. The eagerness drained from her face, as it always did, at the sight of her husband; she lowered her head and glanced uneasily at Betsy. Betsy, dressed in the height of the latest fashion, in a hat that towered somewhere over her head like a lampshade, in a blue dress with violet stripes slanting one way on the bodice and the other on the skirt, sat next to Anna, her tall, flat figure held very straight. Bending her head, she greeted Alexey Alexandrovitch with an ironical smile.

"Ah!" she said, as though surprised. "I'm so glad you're home. You're never to be seen anywhere, and I haven't seen you since Anna fell ill. I've heard all about it — your devotion. Yes, you're a remarkable husband!" she said, with a knowing, affable air, as though awarding him an order of magnanimity for his conduct toward his wife.
Alexey Alexandrovitch bowed coldly, and kissing his wife's hand, asked how she was.
"Better, I think," she said, avoiding his eyes.
"But you've a rather feverish-looking color," he said, stressing the word "feverish."
"We've been talking too much," said Betsy. "It's selfish of me, I know, and I'm going to go."
She stood up, but Anna, suddenly flushing, quickly caught at her hand.
"No — wait a minute, please. I have to tell you... no, you." She turned to Alexey Alexandrovitch, and her neck and brow flushed crimson. "I won't and can't keep anything secret from you," she said.
Alexey Alexandrovitch cracked his fingers and bowed his head.

"Betsy was just telling me that Count Vronsky wants to come here to say good-bye before his departure for Tashkend." She didn't look at her husband, and was clearly in a hurry to get the whole thing out, however hard it was for her. "I told her I couldn't receive him."
"You said, my dear, that it would depend on Alexey Alexandrovitch," Betsy corrected her.
"Oh, no — I can't receive him; and what purpose would there...." She broke off and glanced inquiringly at her husband (he was not looking at her). "In short, I don't wish it...."
Alexey Alexandrovitch stepped forward and would have taken her hand.
Her first impulse was to jerk her hand back from the damp hand with its big swollen veins that was reaching for hers, but with an obvious effort to control herself she pressed his hand.

"I'm very grateful to you for your confidence, but...." he said, feeling, with confusion and irritation, that what he could decide easily and clearly on his own, he could not discuss in front of Princess Tverskaya, who represented for him the incarnation of that brute force that would inevitably control him in the life he led in the eyes of the world, and would block him from giving way to his feeling of love and forgiveness. He broke off, looking at Princess Tverskaya.
"Well, good-bye, my darling," said Betsy, getting up. She kissed Anna and went out. Alexey Alexandrovitch saw her out.

"Alexey Alexandrovitch! I know you are a truly magnanimous man," said Betsy, stopping in the little drawing room and, with special warmth, shaking his hand again. "I'm an outsider, but I love her so much, and respect you so much, that I take the liberty of giving you advice. Receive him. Alexey Vronsky is the soul of honor, and he's leaving for Tashkend."
"Thank you, princess, for your sympathy and your advice. But the question of whom my wife can or cannot receive she must decide for herself."

He said this from habit, lifting his brows with dignity, and immediately reflected that whatever words he used, there could be no dignity in his position. And he saw as much from the suppressed, malicious, ironic smile Betsy gave him after this remark.
